title: Seeing What We Expect
text:
Most people believe that they form opinions by weighing evidence and following it wherever it leads. In practice, the process often runs the other way. Once we have adopted a view, we tend to notice information that supports it and to overlook, dismiss or forget information that challenges it. Psychologists call this tendency confirmation bias, and it affects the educated as much as anyone else.

The bias shows itself in small ways. A supporter of a political party reads a report of a scandal and concludes that the opposing party is corrupt, while a similar report about his own party strikes him as exaggerated. A manager who has formed a poor impression of an employee notices every mistake and passes over every success. In each case, the same kind of evidence is judged by different standards depending on whether it fits an existing belief.

Modern information habits can strengthen the tendency. When people choose their own news sources and follow only like-minded voices, they may meet few serious challenges to their views, and each confirming story makes them more certain. Disagreement then begins to seem not merely mistaken but incomprehensible.

Complete freedom from bias is probably impossible, but its effects can be reduced. One useful habit is to ask, before accepting a claim, what evidence would change one’s mind. Another is to seek out the strongest version of an opposing argument rather than its weakest. Institutions can help too: courts hear both sides before deciding, and scientists submit their work to critical review. Such practices exist precisely because individual judgement, left to itself, is less impartial than it feels.

title: When a Language Falls Silent
text:
Somewhere in the world, a language is spoken fluently by only a handful of elderly people. Their grandchildren understand a few words but reply in the language of school, television and the market. When the last fluent speakers die, the language will survive, at best, in recordings and word lists. Linguists warn that a large share of the world’s languages may meet this fate within the coming century.

Languages rarely disappear because people are forced to abandon them at gunpoint, although that has happened. More often the process is gradual and, in a sense, voluntary. Parents who see that jobs and respect belong to speakers of a dominant language choose to raise their children in it, hoping to spare them disadvantage. Each decision is understandable; together they end a tradition that may have lasted thousands of years.

What is lost is more than a set of words. A language carries a community’s songs, proverbs, jokes and ways of classifying the world. Some languages have detailed vocabularies for local plants, winds or kinds of snow, knowledge accumulated over generations of close observation. When the language goes, much of that knowledge goes with it.

Efforts at revival have had mixed results. Schools that teach in the local language, radio programmes, dictionaries and mobile applications can help, but only if speakers themselves value the language and use it at home. Bilingualism offers a middle path: a child can master a national or international language for work while keeping the language of his grandparents for family and community life. Learning one need not mean forgetting the other.

title: The Traffic of Words
text:
No language lives in isolation. Whenever peoples trade, travel, conquer or simply live side by side, words pass between them as readily as goods. English, often thought of as a single national tongue, is in fact a vast storehouse of borrowings. From the languages of South Asia alone it has taken words such as “bungalow”, “pyjama” and “shampoo”, most of them acquired during the long period of British involvement in the region. Urdu, in turn, has absorbed “school”, “ticket” and “hospital” so thoroughly that many speakers no longer think of them as foreign.

Borrowing usually follows need or prestige. A community adopts a word when it meets a new object or idea for which it has no name of its own, or when the language of a powerful or fashionable group seems to lend an air of sophistication. Over time, the borrowed word is reshaped to fit the sounds and grammar of its new home, and its meaning may drift far from the original.

Purists sometimes regard such borrowing as a kind of decay and call for foreign words to be replaced by native ones. Their concern is not wholly unfounded: when a language borrows for prestige rather than need, it may abandon perfectly good words of its own. Yet attempts to seal a language off from outside influence have rarely succeeded, and a language that borrows freely can gain in richness what it seems to lose in purity.

A dictionary, seen in this light, is a record of history. Each borrowed word marks a moment of contact, a meeting of peoples that left its trace not in stone but in speech.

title: The Schoolmaster of the Valley
text:
When Ghulam Rasool returned to his mountain village after completing his studies in the city, his relatives assumed he would soon leave again. Educated young men, they said, did not stay where the road ended and the winter snows cut the valley off for weeks. He surprised them all. In a borrowed room beside the mosque, with a blackboard he had carried up the path on his back, he opened a school for the village children.

The early years were hard. Many families needed their children in the fields and saw little use in reading. Ghulam Rasool did not argue with them. Instead, he taught in the evenings, after the day’s work was done, and he walked from house to house reading letters aloud for those who could not. Slowly, parents began to see what literacy could do: a son who could check the shopkeeper’s accounts, a daughter who could read the instructions on a bottle of medicine.

He insisted from the start that girls should learn alongside boys. Some elders objected, but he won them over by inviting them to sit in on lessons and see for themselves. Within a decade, his first pupils were teaching younger children, and a small library, built from donated books, occupied a corner of the room.

He never became wealthy or known beyond the valley. When he died, however, his funeral was attended by doctors, engineers, teachers and farmers who had learned their letters under him. On the wall of the school that now bears his name hangs the old blackboard, its surface worn pale by years of chalk.

subject: English
q: The passage is mainly about:
o: the causes of political scandals
methods of evaluating employees
the history of scientific review
the tendency to favour evidence that supports existing beliefs
explanation: The passage explains confirmation bias, the habit of noticing information that supports our views and dismissing what challenges them.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, the example of the manager shows that:
o: managers are usually fair to their employees
employees make more mistakes than successes
the same kind of evidence can be judged differently depending on prior beliefs
first impressions are generally accurate
explanation: The manager notices every mistake and passes over every success; the author concludes that evidence is judged by different standards depending on existing belief.

subject: English
q: Which habit does the passage recommend for reducing the effects of bias?
o: Following only like-minded news sources
Studying the weakest version of opposing arguments
Asking what evidence would change one’s mind
Avoiding all discussion of politics
explanation: The final paragraph recommends asking what evidence would change one’s mind and seeking the strongest opposing argument.

subject: English
q: The word ‘impartial’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: well informed
quick to decide
deeply emotional
fair and unbiased
explanation: Individual judgement is “less impartial than it feels” because it is affected by bias; impartial means fair and free from bias.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred that courts and scientific review are mentioned as examples of:
o: bodies that are completely free from bias
places where confirmation bias is strongest
institutions designed to compensate for the limits of individual judgement
alternatives to gathering evidence
explanation: The author says such practices exist precisely because individual judgement, left to itself, is less impartial than it feels.

subject: English
q: The author’s attitude towards human judgement is best described as:
o: confident that it is naturally impartial
convinced that bias can be eliminated entirely
realistic about its weaknesses but hopeful that they can be reduced
dismissive of any effort to improve it
explanation: The author says complete freedom from bias is probably impossible but that its effects can be reduced by habits and institutions.

subject: English
q: The central concern of the passage is:
o: the difficulty of learning a second language
the spread of mobile applications in schools
the forced removal of communities from their land
the gradual loss of minority languages and what disappears with them
explanation: The passage describes how small languages die out, why it happens, what knowledge is lost and how revival might work.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why do many parents raise their children in a dominant language?
o: They are ordered to do so by law
They have forgotten their own language
They hope to spare them disadvantage in work and status
They find the dominant language easier to speak
explanation: The second paragraph says parents see that jobs and respect belong to speakers of the dominant language and hope to spare their children disadvantage.

subject: English
q: The passage mentions vocabularies for local plants, winds and snow to show that a language:
o: is used mainly for describing the weather
cannot survive without a written dictionary
changes rapidly from one generation to the next
preserves knowledge gathered through long observation
explanation: These vocabularies are described as knowledge accumulated over generations of close observation, which is lost when the language goes.

subject: English
q: The word ‘revival’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: recording for archives
restoration to active use
translation into other languages
gradual abandonment
explanation: Efforts at revival, such as teaching and broadcasting in the language, aim to bring a declining language back into living use.

subject: English
q: The author calls the process of language loss ‘in a sense, voluntary’ because:
o: it results from many individual choices rather than from direct force
speakers deliberately wish their language to die
governments invite communities to abandon their languages
linguists advise communities to adopt dominant languages
explanation: The author contrasts force “at gunpoint” with parents’ understandable decisions, which together end the language without anyone intending it.

subject: English
q: The author’s attitude towards bilingualism is best described as:
o: hostile, seeing it as a threat to national unity
indifferent, seeing it as irrelevant to the problem
doubtful, seeing it as too difficult for children
favourable, seeing it as a practical middle path
explanation: The author presents bilingualism as a middle path and says learning one language need not mean forgetting the other.

subject: English
q: The main idea of the passage is that:
o: English is the only language that borrows words
languages continually borrow words through contact between peoples
borrowed words always keep their original meaning
foreign words should be removed from every language
explanation: The passage explains that words pass between languages wherever peoples meet, with examples from English and Urdu, and treats borrowing as a record of that contact.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, a community usually adopts a foreign word because of:
o: orders from the government
a shortage of dictionaries
pressure from purists
need or prestige
explanation: The second paragraph opens by stating that borrowing usually follows need or prestige.

subject: English
q: What does the passage say happens to a borrowed word over time?
o: It is eventually replaced by a native word
It returns to the language it came from
It keeps its original pronunciation unchanged
It is reshaped to fit the sounds and grammar of its new language
explanation: The passage says the borrowed word is reshaped to fit the sounds and grammar of its new home, and its meaning may drift.

subject: English
q: The word ‘purists’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: scholars who compile dictionaries
traders who travel between countries
writers who invent new words
people who want a language kept free of foreign elements
explanation: Purists regard borrowing as decay and want foreign words replaced by native ones, so they wish to keep the language “pure”.

subject: English
q: The author’s attitude towards the purists’ view is best described as:
o: wholly supportive
openly contemptuous
entirely indifferent
partly sympathetic but ultimately unconvinced
explanation: The author grants that their concern is “not wholly unfounded” but argues that sealing a language off rarely succeeds and that borrowing brings richness.

subject: English
q: The author calls a dictionary ‘a record of history’ because:
o: dictionaries are usually written by historians
every word in a dictionary is very old
borrowed words preserve traces of past contact between peoples
dictionaries list the dates of important events
explanation: Each borrowed word marks a moment of contact, a meeting of peoples that left its trace in speech.

subject: English
q: The passage is chiefly about:
o: the hardships of winter in mountain villages
a teacher’s patient efforts to bring education to his village
a young man’s successful career in the city
the building of a road to a remote valley
explanation: The passage follows Ghulam Rasool from opening a school in a borrowed room to the lasting influence of his teaching.

subject: English
q: Why did Ghulam Rasool’s relatives expect him to leave the village again?
o: They believed educated young men did not stay in such remote places
He had been offered a teaching post in the city
The village elders had opposed his return
His family needed him to work elsewhere
explanation: The relatives said educated young men did not stay where the road ended and the snows cut the valley off.

subject: English
q: How did Ghulam Rasool persuade the elders who objected to girls’ education?
o: He offered their families free books
He threatened to close the school
He invited them to sit in on lessons and see for themselves
He asked the city authorities to intervene
explanation: The third paragraph says he won the elders over by inviting them to sit in on lessons and see for themselves.

subject: English
q: The expression ‘won them over’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: defeated them
persuaded them
rewarded them
ignored them
explanation: The elders objected, but he changed their minds by letting them observe lessons, so “won them over” means persuaded them.

subject: English
q: The detail of the old blackboard hanging on the school wall suggests that:
o: the school cannot afford new equipment
the blackboard is still used for daily lessons
Ghulam Rasool asked for it to be kept as a gift
the village honours the modest beginnings of its school
explanation: The school now bears his name and displays the worn blackboard he once carried up the path, a mark of respect for how the school began.

subject: English
q: The tone of the passage is best described as:
o: critical and ironic
detached and clinical
warm and admiring
angry and bitter
explanation: The narrative dwells on the teacher’s patience, persistence and lasting influence with evident respect.
